analysis.one_liner: Strikes down state bans and restrictions on abortion before fetal viability and protects travel for care.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2025 with 209 of 217 House Democrats signed on, but the bill has seen no committee action or vote in the Republican-led House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar governments — federal, state, and local — from banning abortion before fetal viability or imposing common restrictions like mandatory waiting visits, required procedures, limits on medication abortion or telemedicine, and hospital-admitting rules that don't apply to comparable procedures. After viability, it protects abortions a treating provider judges necessary for the patient's life or health. It also recognizes a right to travel between states for care, and lets the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue states that violate it. It passed nothing: it was referred to two House committees and has sat there since.
analysis.who_benefits: People who can become pregnant — especially those in the 14 states where abortion is unavailable in their home state, and low-income people who cannot easily travel hundreds of miles or take days off work. Providers whose clinics closed after the Dobbs decision would also gain a federal right to practice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant people, especially in ban states

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits governments from banning abortion before fetal viability and from imposing requirements like unnecessary in-person visits, medically inaccurate counseling scripts, or facility and credentialing rules not applied to medically comparable procedures.
Protects abortions after viability when a treating provider judges them necessary to protect the patient's life or health, and lets states go further if they choose.
Recognizes a right to interstate travel, including for abortion services, and a right to help someone else obtain care.
Gives the Justice Department, patients, and providers a private right of action to sue states and officials enforcing violating laws, overriding state sovereign immunity.

The bill's findings state that as of January 2025, abortion is unavailable in 14 states, leaving 17.98 million women of reproductive age without access in their home state, and that travel time to a clinic has quadrupled since Dobbs — burdens of lost wages, transportation, lodging, and child care that fall hardest on low-income people.

analysis.who_pays: State governments in ban states would lose their authority to restrict abortion and would face lawsuits; the federal government would bear enforcement costs through Justice Department litigation. People opposed to abortion on moral grounds would see state bans they supported struck down nationwide.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws adopted through the democratic process — including bans enacted by state legislatures and, in some states, approved by voters — replacing state policy with a single federal standard defined largely by the treating provider's medical judgment.

It defines viability by the provider's good-faith judgment and defines the 'health' exception after viability broadly, which critics say goes beyond the post-viability limits of the pre-Dobbs framework and would be tested hard in court under the commerce clause and Fourteenth Amendment authorities the bill invokes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states where abortion is banned, the bill would restore access that millions lost after Dobbs and remove travel burdens that fall hardest on those with low incomes. The genuine cost is to state self-government: it would override state abortion laws nationwide, including ones passed by referendum, and its pre- and post-viability standards rest on provider judgment rather than fixed legal lines. Whether that trade is acceptable is the core political disagreement; the bill makes its position explicit rather than ambiguous.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 24, 2025, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, and has sat in committee since with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Judy Chu introduced the Women's Health Protection Act of 2025 in the House on June 24, 2025.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to the Judiciary Committee.
209 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The full action history shows only introduction and committee referral, with no further action to date.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, state abortion bans and restrictions remain in force; states with bans and opponents of abortion access are better off with the status quo than they would be if it became law.

sides.party_line_note: All 209 cosponsors are House Democrats — 209 of the 217-member caucus — and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill has stayed in committee.

industries.note: The bill would restore legal protection for their services nationwide and undo state bans, reopening a closed market in 14 states. Patients gain access at the same time providers regain a line of business.

industries.industry: Hospitals, pharmacies, and general health care providers
industries.note: The bill's findings say clinicians and pharmacists in restrictive states have been unable to dispense drugs also used for medication abortion, and patients have been delayed in miscarriage and ectopic-pregnancy care; federal preemption would remove that legal risk for routine care.

industries.industry: Anti-abortion pregnancy centers and counseling organizations
industries.note: The bill bars governments from enforcing many state measures these organizations support, and its catch-all provision restricts measures that 'impede access' to abortion, narrowing the policy space they operate in.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans controlling the House, the Senate, and the White House, the bill is unlikely to get committee action or a floor vote in this Congress. This bill's typical path is repeated reintroduction in each Congress as a statement of position, awaiting a chamber aligned with its supporters.
